The long term forecast period starts out on a seasonably hot note in 
Eastern Kentucky, with synoptic conditions favoring efficient 
diurnal warming. When the period opens on Monday morning, the area 
will be positioned between a building ridge over the Southern Plains 
and the subtropical ridge over the southeastern states. Models 
collectively resolve midlevel height rises over the commonwealth on 
Monday as the influence of the former feature grows. Both diabatic 
and adiabatic warming processes will allow temperatures to climb 
towards the upper 80s/lower 90s on Monday. These seasonably hot 
highs will combine with the antecedent moisture (dewpoints in the 
70s) to yield widespread heat indices in the 90s. A few triple digit 
readings cannot be ruled out, but heat headline products are not 
anticipated. 

This partially due to increased rain chances on Monday in southern 
portions of the forecast area, which may cause localized pockets of 
rain-cooled air and cause highs to under-perform. As the col 
previously noted between the two synoptic ridges closes up on 
Monday, it will push a subtle upper level disturbance towards the 
Tennessee River Valley. This feature's alignment with peak diurnal 
heating has introduced isolated to scattered coverage PoPs (15-35%) 
across the counties along the TN and VA state lines. Due to the 
previously-discussed and increasing influence of the dominant 
ridging features, this activity should not pose a risk for any 
significant impacts. Rather, a few run-of-the-mill late summertime 
showers and thunderstorms cannot be ruled out on Monday 
afternoon/evening.  

The flow aloft is progged to turn more northwesterly overnight into 
Tuesday morning, which will allow a series of shortwave impulses to 
navigate around the ridge and into the forecast area. Pattern 
recognition suggests that the convection associated with these 
disturbances could take the form of MCSes moving through the Midwest 
and the Greater Ohio River Valley. The first of those thunderstorm 
complexes could affect far northern portions of the forecast area 
late Monday night into Tuesday morning, and SPC has accordingly 
delineated a Marginal (Level 1/5) Severe Weather Outlook in Fleming 
and Rowan Counties for the period ending at 8AM Tuesday. Damaging 
wind gusts would be the primary hazard type in this type of setup, 
but it is uncertain how strong each complex will be by the time it 
arrives in the JKL CWA. The first one will be arriving during the 
diurnal instability minima, and it will probably be in a weakening 
state as a result. It remains difficult to pinpoint the timing 
details surrounding each shortwave, and it is equally difficult to 
determine where any residual outflow boundaries and/or instability 
gradients might set up in the wake of each storm complex. Forecast 
uncertainty accordingly compounds as the week progresses.

With that being said, interests are encouraged to remain weather 
aware on Tuesday and Wednesday. The available medium-range machine 
learning models and analog-based convective guidance still paint 
risks for severe weather across portions of Eastern Kentucky on 
these two days. Once again, damaging wind gusts would be the favored 
hazard type in such a setup, but mesoscale effects could cause the 
favored risk areas to shift and other convective hazards cannot 
entirely be ruled out. Any severe weather risk will be accompanied 
by a threat for excessive rainfall, and WPC has already delineated a 
Slight (Level 2/4) Excessive Rainfall Outlooks for portions of the 
commonwealth on both Tuesday and Wednesday. Flash flooding could 
develop if storms engage in training and/or backbuilding behaviors. 
Given the compounding nature of the forecast uncertainty surrounding 
this setup, it is too early to advertise specific rainfall totals. 
Instead, we will need to monitor the output of higher-resolution 
forecast models for parameter spacing that favors those behaviors. 
The first MCS enters the temporal range of the long-range CAMs 
tonight, and as more data becomes available in the coming days, 
forecast confidence should improve. 

All of this activity will culminate in the approach of a cold front 
towards the end of the period. In general, increased late week cloud 
cover should work to suppress the early week heat as time passes. 
Temperatures are forecast to modulate back towards more 
climatologically-appropriate values by Thursday. Expect highs to 
return to the mid/low 80s on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday and lows 
to fall somewhere between the mid 60s and near 70. Precipitation 
chances are more uncertain, as the extended forecast guidance suite 
is split on how progressive that boundary will be. If it is slower
